title: The Last Oath Again
premise: Yara Hartwell, a cartographer who maps realms that shouldn't exist, discovers the ledgers of the Guild of Impossible Things record a debt older than the guild itself: a soul sold generations ago to the court beneath the mountain, and that soul belongs to Yara's own bloodline. When the old gods resume answering prayers, their returning power threatens to extinguish the last dragon-fire — the only force that can unmake a bargain sealed in divine law. Yara must betray the guild that raised them, descend into the mountain court with a disgraced oath-keeper and a god in disguise, and steal back the soul before the fire gutters out. In the end, Yara learns loyalty to truth matters more than belonging to any institution, pays the debt with their own name instead of blood, and rewrites the ledgers so no one is ever sold again.
about_author: Marguerite Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing medieval trade contracts before turning to fiction. She writes fantasy about paperwork, promises, and the people caught between them.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Debts
chapters.summary: Yara Hartwell, POV. While auditing the guild's oldest ledgers, Yara finds an entry written in their grandmother's hand: one soul, sold beneath the mountain, payment deferred. The emotional beat is quiet dread — the discovery that family history is a contract.

chapters.title: Prayers Answered
chapters.summary: Yara, POV. Across the city, old gods begin answering prayers again; a shrine Yara passes grants a stranger's wish at terrible cost. The guild orders all maps of divine territory burned. Beat: wonder curdling into fear as the impossible becomes policy.

chapters.title: The Oath-Keeper's Fall
chapters.summary: Davor Ashling, POV. A disgraced oath-keeper who once enforced the soul-contract arrives demanding the ledger page. Yara refuses; Davor reveals the last dragon-fire is guttering and the contract will auto-execute when it dies. Beat: reluctant alliance born of mutual shame.

chapters.title: What the Guild Keeps
chapters.summary: Yara, POV. Yara searches the guild vault for the original seal and finds the masters have been feeding prayers to the mountain court for centuries, buying stability with other people's souls. Beat: betrayal — belonging revealed as complicity.

chapters.title: A God in Disguise
chapters.summary: Sef, POV. A humble guild clerk is revealed as a minor old god hiding from his siblings' return; he offers Yara passage beneath the mountain in exchange for being forgotten again. Beat: strange tenderness between the mortal and the divine.

chapters.title: The Descent
chapters.summary: Yara, POV. Yara, Davor, and Sef travel through unmapped caverns Yara must chart as they go, pursued by guild hunters. Davor confesses he signed the original sale. Beat: trust forged in darkness, literally and morally.

chapters.title: The Court Beneath
chapters.summary: Yara, POV. The mountain court receives them with courtesy that is worse than cruelty; Yara sees their grandmother's soul, still bound, still aware. Beat: horror tempered by love — the debt has a face.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Davor, POV. Negotiations collapse when the court demands a living heir in exchange; Davor offers himself to honor his broken oath, but divine law rejects a willing sacrifice. Beat: despair — loyalty alone cannot pay what truth owes.

chapters.title: The Last Dragon-Fire
chapters.summary: Yara, POV. As the final flame gutters, Yara invokes an ancient clause: debts may be paid in name rather than blood. Yara surrenders 'Hartwell,' erasing their lineage from every ledger, freeing the soul and binding the court to honesty. Climax: self-erasure as both loss and liberation.

chapters.title: Rewritten
chapters.summary: Yara, POV. The dragon-fire steadies; the grandmother's soul departs in peace; the guild masters face reckoning. Nameless but not lost, Yara begins a new ledger with a single rule: nothing that breathes shall be collateral. Resolution: inheritance redefined as responsibility, not property.
